paragraphs: The paper addresses classification tasks in which one example can belong to several categories. Its motivating application is assigning functions to yeast genes. The authors argue that the usual strategy of breaking a multilabel problem into many separate binary decisions can have limited expressive power, motivating a method that handles the labeling problem more directly.

Their proposed learning system uses large-margin ranking and shares several properties with support vector machines. The central change is to organize learning around ranking labels, rather than treating every category decision as a separate two-class problem. This gives the method a way to address the relative ordering of labels within a common learning formulation.

The authors report positive results on yeast gene functional classification. That finding supports the usefulness of their direct ranking approach in the stated application. The contribution is a different formulation of multilabel learning: it brings the large-margin perspective associated with SVMs to a setting where a single exclusive class assignment is insufficient.
neurips-2001-a-kernel-method-for-multi-l.tldr: The paper proposes an SVM-like large-margin ranking method for multilabel classification and reports positive results on yeast gene functions.

paragraphs: The paper develops a natural gradient method for improving a policy, the rule a learning agent uses to choose actions. Its update direction reflects the underlying structure of the parameter space. This makes the meaning of steepest improvement depend on that structure, rather than only on the numerical coordinates used to describe the policy.

The authors connect this direction to policy iteration. Although gradient methods make limited changes to parameter values, they show that the natural gradient moves toward the greedy actions associated with one policy-improvement step. This relationship uses approximate value functions satisfying a compatibility requirement. The claim concerns the direction of improvement under that formulation, rather than an immediate jump to a globally optimal policy.

Experiments show drastic performance improvements in simple Markov decision processes and in Tetris, a more challenging decision problem. Together, the theoretical connection and experiments explain why the update can be useful: a local parameter change can point toward a stronger policy-improvement target than merely favoring a somewhat better action.
neurips-2001-a-natural-policy-gradient-f.tldr: A natural policy gradient follows the structure of policy parameter space toward a policy-iteration improvement target, with large reported performance gains.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the computational cost of training support vector machines on very large datasets. The authors describe training complexity that grows at least quadratically with the number of examples, making a single large training problem difficult to manage. Their aim is to retain SVM-based classification while changing how the training work is organized.

They propose a mixture of SVMs in which each component learns from a small subset of the complete dataset. The mixture is designed for straightforward parallel implementation. Dividing the data among smaller training problems addresses the size of each individual optimization task while also allowing those tasks to be carried out concurrently.

Experiments on the Forest benchmark and a difficult speech database show significant training-time improvements. Over the ranges examined, time complexity appears locally linear in dataset size; this is an empirical observation, not a general scaling guarantee. The authors also report a surprising improvement in generalization on Forest, showing that the observed benefit there extended beyond faster training.
neurips-2001-a-parallel-mixture-of-svms-.tldr: A parallel mixture of SVMs trained on smaller data subsets substantially reduces training time and also improves generalization on Forest.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people adjust their behavior when rapidly classifying a sequence of stimuli. When one stimulus class appears less often, responses to that class become slower and more error-prone. The authors ask how cognitive control responds to these unequal frequencies and how one account can explain both response speed and accuracy.

Their model treats performance as an attempt to minimize a cost that includes both errors and reaction time. It adds two assumptions: people accurately estimate the class probabilities, and their inference is optimal subject to a limit on how quickly information can be transmitted. Rational behavior therefore operates within an explicit processing constraint.

With these assumptions, the model fits overall reaction-time and error patterns well, including changes from one trial to the next. The result supports an explanation linking task frequencies, processing limits, and the cost of responding. It shows how the reported performance patterns can be understood through constrained optimization, rather than treating speed and accuracy as unrelated outcomes.
neurips-2001-a-rational-analysis-of-cogn.tldr: A model balancing errors and response time fits discrimination-task behavior under assumptions of accurate class probabilities and information-limited optimal inference.

paragraphs: The paper presents an analog circuit for flexible pattern matching, paired with an image representation method called Principal Axes Projection, or PAP. The system combines a preprocessing stage that extracts image features with a hardware stage that evaluates similarity. This connects the way an image is encoded to the circuit that classifies its resulting representation.

The matching response can be configured through its peak position, peak height, and sharpness. These controls change where the similarity response is strongest, how strong that response is, and how narrowly it is concentrated. That flexibility is central to the proposed soft-matching classifier because the form of the similarity evaluation is adjustable.

The authors fabricated a test chip and successfully applied it to handwritten pattern recognition and medical radiograph analysis, using PAP for robust image coding. They also experimentally demonstrated separation and classification of overlapping patterns. These results establish operation in physical hardware and show the combined representation-and-classification approach working in the reported image tasks.
neurips-2001-analog-soft-pattern-matchin.tldr: An adjustable analog similarity circuit, combined with Principal Axes Projection, demonstrates recognition of handwritten, radiographic, and overlapping patterns.

paragraphs: The paper presents three methods for approximating value functions in reinforcement learning using linear programming and kernels. A value function supplies evaluations that help an agent choose actions. The shared aim is to fit the available data while keeping the number of support vectors small, linking the quality of the approximation to the size of its representation.

The three formulations impose different demands on learning. One follows support vector regression, another uses the Bellman equation, and a third asks only that good moves receive an advantage over bad moves. The last formulation focuses on the distinction needed for choosing between actions, rather than requiring the same kind of value fit as the other approaches.

All three perform excellently on a difficult synthetic maze problem, but the advantage formulation is much easier to train. The authors also emphasize that these kernel methods can readily adjust approximator complexity to value-function complexity. The reported results make the training objective an important practical choice even among methods with strong task performance.
neurips-2001-batch-value-function-approx.tldr: Three kernel-based value approximators perform strongly on a synthetic maze, with an action-advantage formulation proving much easier to train.

paragraphs: The paper asks how historical transaction records can be turned into predictive profiles for individuals. Such records arise routinely in retail, telecommunications, and website management. The task is to use a person's recorded behavior to anticipate future behavior, while also drawing on regularities found across the wider population.

The authors build a generative mixture model for count data and estimate it using an approximate Bayesian framework. The mixture represents population patterns, while the Bayesian estimation combines those patterns with an individual's own history. The resulting profile therefore incorporates both sources of information within one predictive modeling approach.

A large real-world retail dataset provides the demonstration. On transactions held out from fitting, the profiles consistently outperform the non-mixture and non-Bayesian techniques considered. This means their advantage concerns predictions on unseen data, rather than only descriptions of past records. The findings support combining population structure and individual evidence when constructing customer profiles in the studied retail setting.
neurips-2001-bayesian-predictive-profile.tldr: Bayesian mixture profiles combine individual histories with population patterns and improve held-out customer-behavior predictions on a large retail dataset.

paragraphs: The paper explains why inferior temporal cortex neurons respond to an object across a large region on a blank background but across a smaller region in a natural scene. This reduction limits recognition across changes in object position. The authors suggest that the smaller effective receptive field may help the visual system select an object amid competing scene content.

Their model combines competition among neurons tuned to different objects with greater cortical representation of the fovea than of peripheral vision. Competition occurs within an attractor network. The model also shows that a top-down bias toward an object can enlarge its receptive field, offering an account of object-based attention during visual search.

A specific prediction follows: adding a second object to an otherwise blank scene should shrink the target's receptive field, with the amount depending on object proximity. The authors further suggest that this mechanism could make the output of inferior temporal cortex primarily describe one object, allowing downstream areas to select it as a possible action target.
neurips-2001-effective-size-of-receptive.tldr: A competitive neural model explains scene-dependent receptive-field shrinkage and predicts how nearby objects and top-down attention change it.

paragraphs: The paper investigates compact representations for face recognition. Conventional Eigenface and Fisherface approaches use second-order image statistics, leaving out higher-order relationships such as dependencies involving three or more pixels. The authors explore whether extending these established subspace methods can produce representations that capture more of the statistical structure relevant to recognizing faces.

They apply Kernel Principal Component Analysis and Kernel Fisher Linear Discriminant, calling the resulting approaches Kernel Eigenface and Kernel Fisherface. These methods generalize the corresponding conventional representations to account for higher-order correlations. The goal remains a low-dimensional description of an image, but the statistical relationships used to construct it are richer.

The evaluation compares the kernel approaches with Eigenface, Fisherface, and independent-component-based methods under changes in pose, scale, lighting, and expression. The reported experiments show better representations and lower recognition error for the kernel methods. These findings support the value of including higher-order image relationships in the tested face-recognition settings, while retaining the compact-representation objective.
neurips-2001-face-recognition-using-kern.tldr: Kernel extensions of Eigenface and Fisherface capture higher-order image relationships and achieve lower face-recognition error in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a model can represent relationships between objects, such as a square being above a triangle. Its approach uses low-order conjunctive representations, which encode combinations of information. The authors address two criticisms of such representations: that they require too many units and that they become too specific to generalize to unfamiliar inputs.

The model uses coarse coding and distributed representations. Each hidden unit responds broadly across a space of possible conjunctions, so the representation of a relationship is spread across units rather than requiring a dedicated unit for every combination. This is the mechanism offered for representing many conjunctions with relatively few hidden units.

The authors show that their model uses far fewer hidden units than the number of conjunctions it represents and achieves considerable generalization to novel inputs. These findings counter the claimed efficiency and generalization problems for this model. They demonstrate a viable way to bind relational information without relying on the temporal synchrony mechanisms discussed as an alternative.
neurips-2001-generalizable-relational-bi.tldr: Distributed, broadly tuned conjunctive representations encode spatial relationships with relatively few units and generalize considerably to novel inputs.

paragraphs: The paper examines generalization for certain learning problems whose predictors belong to Hilbert spaces of functions. Its central comparison is between a predictor estimated through learning and the best underlying predictor. This frames the analysis around how closely the learned function approaches that target, rather than only how well it fits the observations used to estimate it.

The authors introduce a notion of convergence for this comparison and obtain an estimate of its rate. Defining convergence specifies what it means for the estimated predictor to approach the target. Estimating the rate adds a quantitative account of that approach, providing more information than a statement that convergence occurs.

They then use the rate estimate to derive generalization bounds for some learning formulations. The contribution is this chain from a definition of predictor convergence to quantitative guarantees about generalization. Its stated scope is particular learning problems and formulations in Hilbert functional spaces; the abstract does not assert that the same bound covers every method in such spaces.
neurips-2001-generalization-performance-.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for some Hilbert-space learning formulations by estimating convergence rates toward the best underlying predictor.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes asymmetric lateral connections as a possible explanation for cortical neurons that prefer particular directions of motion. It studies a class of recurrent networks while explicitly accounting for neuronal thresholds. This allows the analysis to address nonlinear dynamics that earlier treatments based on linear systems methods did not capture.

The authors show that these networks support traveling pulses of activity that remain locked to a moving stimulus. Such solutions are appropriate for modeling direction-selective responses. However, their stability holds only within a certain range of stimulus speeds. Outside that range, the stable behavior gives way to another class of solutions with specific repeating patterns in space and time.

The resulting prediction is conditional: if asymmetric lateral connections are the main source of cortical direction selectivity, suitable stimulus speeds might produce observable lurching activity waves. The analysis therefore connects a proposed circuit mechanism to a distinctive population-level pattern, providing more than a description of a single neuron's preferred direction.
neurips-2001-generating-velocity-tuning-.tldr: Nonlinear analysis of asymmetric recurrent networks predicts stimulus-locked pulses and, conditionally, lurching activity waves outside a stable speed range.

paragraphs: The paper develops a support vector machine training framework using parametric quadratic programming. It separates the optimization into two related methods centered on the bias parameter. One solves the training problem while keeping that bias fixed; the other begins with an optimal fixed-bias solution and adjusts the bias until its optimal value is reached.

The bias-adjustment method can work with any existing technique that supplies a fixed-bias solution. It can also solve the complete SVM training problem independently. This gives the framework several ways to organize training, including combining the two proposed methods rather than committing to either one alone.

The authors state that the combination yields an incremental algorithm that exactly solves the 1-norm soft-margin SVM optimization problem. Exactness here concerns the specified optimization objective. They also suggest that selective sampling may improve convergence further. That additional benefit is presented as a possibility, whereas the exact incremental solution is a stated property of the combined approach.
neurips-2001-incremental-learning-and-se.tldr: A parametric optimization framework combines fixed-bias solving and bias adjustment to exactly train a 1-norm soft-margin SVM incrementally.

paragraphs: The paper develops supervised learning for the lateral interactions in a competitive layer model, a recurrent network used for dynamic feature binding. These interactions help determine how features are organized through the network's activity. The task is to learn their weights from examples so that the network's resulting organization supports the intended segmentation.

The method uses consistency conditions that characterize the network's attractor states, the states associated with its settled behavior. Those conditions allow training to be expressed as a convex quadratic optimization problem over the interaction weights. This connects the desired recurrent behavior to a structured optimization problem that can be solved during learning.

The authors also reduce the dimension of the problem by expressing interactions as linear combinations of basis interactions. They demonstrate successful application to segmentation of cells in fluorescence microscope images. The contribution joins a characterization of network dynamics with a practical learning formulation, and the image application shows that this formulation can support the reported sensory-segmentation task.
neurips-2001-learning-lateral-interactio.tldr: Attractor consistency conditions turn supervised learning of recurrent lateral interactions into convex quadratic optimization, demonstrated on microscope cell segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper presents a fabricated silicon synapse that learns a conditional probability or correlation between spike-based inputs and feedback signals. The device combines learning and computation in one circuit: it can multiply signals while adapting its stored weight. The authors describe it as compact and low power, with weight storage that persists without continuous power.

Arrays of these synapses can be calibrated to have uniform adaptation characteristics. Another feature is that the signals driving adaptation need not be the same ones used for computation. This flexibility allows learning rules that relate earlier synaptic activity to present activity, broadening the temporal relationships the hardware can learn.

The paper supplies circuit analysis and experimental chip results for both learning and calibration modes. It also explains how the synapse can implement several learning rules in silicon. The evidence therefore concerns an operating physical device, while the architectural contribution is a synapse whose computation, persistent storage, and adaptation can be used together.
neurips-2001-learning-spike-based-correl.tldr: A fabricated low-power synapse learns spike-based probabilities or correlations while supporting persistent weights, simultaneous computation, and calibrated adaptation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses whether complex movement can be described through combinations of a few reusable elements. It focuses on muscle synergies: coordinated activity patterns across muscles that have been proposed as building blocks of motor control. The authors develop a model in which those patterns have both an amplitude structure and a structure over time.

Making a synergy time-varying allows the building block itself to describe an unfolding pattern of muscle activity. Combining such elements provides a proposed basis for decomposing the complex muscle patterns seen in natural behavior. The model therefore treats temporal organization as part of each component rather than describing coordination only through muscle activation levels.

To extract these components from simultaneous electromyographic recordings, the authors develop an extension of non-negative matrix factorization. This supplies a computational method for finding the proposed time-varying synergies in recorded muscle activity. The contribution is a model and extraction algorithm for examining modular organization; the abstract presents synergies as possible biological building blocks.
neurips-2001-modularity-in-the-motor-sys.tldr: The paper models muscle activity as combinations of time-varying synergies and extends non-negative matrix factorization to extract them from EMG.

paragraphs: The paper tackles blind source separation when the sources do not satisfy the independence assumption used by standard independent component analysis. Instead of considering individual sample amplitudes alone, it groups neighboring samples into patches. It first extracts independent features from observed patches, seeking a representation in which cross-source dependencies are easier to isolate.

The authors find that average dependencies between corresponding features across sources are generally lower than dependencies between source amplitudes. They also show that much of the remaining dependence may be concentrated in only a few features. If those features can be identified heuristically, the method projects patches away from the subspace they span.

Standard ICA is then applied to the transformed patches, whose elements satisfy the independence assumption in the described case. The authors report that this robustly estimates the mixing matrix. The approach depends on dependence being concentrated in identifiable features: it offers a conditional route from correlated sources to a representation suitable for conventional ICA.
neurips-2001-multi-dimensional-ica-to-se.tldr: Patch-based feature removal can enable ICA for correlated sources when their dependence is concentrated in a small, identifiable feature subspace.

paragraphs: The paper studies how reliably spectral properties can be estimated from a random sample of data points. Its focus includes individual eigenvalues and the sum of the smaller eigenvalues in the spectrum's tail. Considering both quantities distinguishes the reliability of individual spectral measurements from the reliability of an aggregate describing the remaining tail.

The authors also analyze residuals produced when data is projected into a subspace. These residuals describe what remains outside the chosen subspace. They show that a random sample can reliably estimate these quantities as well, connecting their spectral analysis to the error associated with representing data in a reduced space.

Experiments confirm the theoretical results reported in the paper. The contribution is a set of reliability statements about measurements made from randomly sampled data, supported by empirical checks. This matters when a sample is used to assess spectral structure or projection quality: the paper addresses whether those observed quantities can provide dependable estimates, rather than merely being computable.
neurips-2001-on-the-concentration-of-spe.tldr: The paper establishes reliable random-sample estimates for eigenvalues, spectral tail sums, and subspace-projection residuals, with supporting experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops theory for co-training and related rule-based bootstrapping methods. These approaches had shown empirical success, but the authors argue that earlier theory was only loosely connected to practically useful algorithms. Their goal is to provide a generalization analysis that addresses choices actually made in these learning procedures.

They derive a PAC-style bound on generalization error that supports using confidence through partial rules and partial labeling of unlabeled examples. This means the analysis accommodates procedures that leave some decisions unresolved instead of forcing a label onto every available example. Confidence therefore has a role in the theoretical account of how the learned system generalizes.

The bound also justifies an objective based on agreement and applies to multiclass classification. Together, these results connect the theory to selective labeling and agreement-driven learning, two concrete features emphasized in the abstract. The stated contribution is a generalization bound supporting these design choices, rather than a new empirical comparison or an unconditional guarantee for every co-training procedure.
neurips-2001-pac-generalization-bounds-f.tldr: New PAC-style co-training bounds support confidence-based partial labeling and agreement objectives, including in multiclass problems.

paragraphs: The supplied abstract frames information search as a problem of navigating networks such as the World Wide Web. It distinguishes centralized indexing from decentralized approaches that move through the network without knowing its global structure. The central issue is how a search proceeds when the participant lacks a complete map of the available connections.

Several settings illustrate that issue. People browse by following hyperlinks, while focused crawlers and other automated agents explore links to collect information. Both involve movement through the network itself. Presenting them together highlights the shared search setting even though one involves human browsing and the other involves automated exploration.

The abstract also connects this perspective to decentralized peer-to-peer systems, where users share resources without a central server. Its stated content establishes a common problem across browsing, crawling, and distributed resource search. The explanatory emphasis is on the information available to a search process and the structure it navigates; the supplied passage sets up that perspective without presenting a particular algorithm or result.
neurips-2001-small-world-phenomena-and-t.tldr: The abstract frames web browsing, crawling, and peer-to-peer resource discovery as decentralized network search without global structural knowledge.

paragraphs: The paper introduces clustering algorithms built around a kernel matrix. For these algorithms, the necessary information is contained in eigenvectors of that matrix or closely related matrices. The approach therefore turns unsupervised learning into a problem that can be addressed through the matrix's spectral structure.

The authors formulate clustering as assigning labels to optimize one of two related objectives, alignment and cut cost. These objectives measure how labels correspond to clusters in the data, with cut cost drawing on graph-theoretic ideas. The labels are the grouping assignments being sought, so the objective supplies a criterion for evaluating possible partitions.

A slight relaxation of the optimization problem leads to an approximation of the optimal solution using eigenvector information. This explains why the spectral calculation is relevant to the labeling objective, rather than introducing it as an unrelated heuristic. The resulting simple algorithms produce positive results on real-world data, supporting the practical usefulness of the relaxed optimization approach in the reported tests.
neurips-2001-spectral-kernel-methods-for.tldr: The paper derives kernel clustering algorithms by relaxing label-assignment objectives into problems solved approximately through eigenvector information.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a packet switch should resolve competition among queued packets for its outputs. The arbitration policy directly affects switch performance, and the best choice depends on both the current switch state and traffic patterns. A useful decision rule therefore needs to account for conditions that change as packets arrive and are served.

The difficulty is the size of the decision problem. As a switch grows, its possible states, transitions, and actions all grow exponentially. Representing and evaluating the entire problem as one large decision system consequently becomes difficult. The authors formulate arbitration as a reinforcement learning problem to address decisions through a value-based framework.

Their key step is to decompose the value function into many small independent value functions. They also provide efficient action selection within this formulation. These contributions address both evaluating situations and choosing what the switch should do. The stated result is a computationally manageable formulation of arbitration, with the decomposition serving as the central response to the expanding decision space.
neurips-2001-switch-packet-arbitration-v.tldr: A reinforcement learning formulation decomposes packet-switch arbitration values into small independent components and enables efficient action selection.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a clustering method connecting scale-space and support-vector clustering ideas. Each data point is associated with a vector in Hilbert space, and the method emphasizes the sum of those vectors. That sum corresponds to the scale-space probability function, providing a shared representation from which the clustering construction begins.

The new step is to study an operator expressed through a Schrödinger equation for which that probability function is a solution. The authors derive the equation's potential function analytically from the probability function and identify potential minima with cluster centers. Thus, the grouping structure is read from a derived potential rather than solely from the original probability representation.

The method has one adjustable parameter, the scale of its Gaussian kernel, and is demonstrated on known datasets. To handle high-dimensional problems, the authors restrict potential evaluation to the observed data locations. This gives a way to apply the construction without evaluating the potential throughout the surrounding high-dimensional space.
neurips-2001-the-method-of-quantum-clust.tldr: Quantum clustering identifies cluster centers as minima of a Schrödinger potential derived from a Gaussian-kernel probability representation.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm for learning models whose junction trees remain thin. Thinness means imposing an upper bound on the largest cliques in the model's triangulated graph. This structural restriction matters because inference must be carried out within the model, and the authors use it to keep that computation tractable.

The restriction is maintained throughout learning, rather than applied only to the completed model. As a result, the authors can efficiently implement an iterative scaling algorithm for estimating parameters. The model structure and the parameter-learning procedure are therefore designed to work together: maintaining manageable inference supports the repeated computations needed during estimation.

The same structural property also allows efficient inference after learning has finished. The authors illustrate the approach through handwritten digit recognition and DNA splice-site detection. The contribution is a model-learning strategy that explicitly controls inference complexity at both stages of use, making tractability a property preserved by the learning process and retained by its final output.
neurips-2001-thin-junction-trees-d2cef82.tldr: Bounding junction-tree clique sizes keeps inference tractable during model learning and in the final learned model.

paragraphs: The paper investigates belief propagation on graphs containing cycles through the problem of two-dimensional phase unwrapping. Phase-wrapped images arise in imaging methods including magnetic resonance imaging and interferometric synthetic aperture radar. The authors propose a new representation of the unwrapping problem and use loopy belief propagation to perform inference within it.

They report results superior to existing techniques. This supplies an application beyond the error-correcting decoding setting that motivates their discussion of loopy inference. The representation is central to the contribution because it makes phase unwrapping a problem on which this inference procedure can be applied successfully.

The graph contains many very short cycles, yet the method still achieves excellent results. That observation supports the conclusion that a large minimum cycle length is not necessary for strong belief-propagation performance. It is evidence from the proposed application, rather than a claim that short cycles are harmless in every graph or that loopy belief propagation always produces accurate inference.
neurips-2001-very-loopy-belief-propagati.tldr: A new phase-unwrapping representation lets loopy belief propagation outperform existing techniques despite having many very short graph cycles.
